title: ALGEBRAIC METHOD FOR APPROXIMATING JOINT STATIONARY DISTRIBUTION IN FINITE CAPACITY QUEUE WITH NEGATIVE CUSTOMERS AND TWO QUEUES

items.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Triggered by earlier work on random walks in the quarter-plane, we study the issue of
                    <jats:italic>two-queue systems</jats:italic>
                    whereby, at least for states (
                    <jats:italic>m</jats:italic>
                    , 
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                    ) in some
                    <jats:italic>interior</jats:italic>
                    part of the state space, the stationary joint system-content distribution
                    <jats:italic>u</jats:italic>
                    (
                    <jats:italic>m</jats:italic>
                    , 
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                    ) can be expressed as a
                    <jats:italic>finite</jats:italic>
                    linear combination of bivariate geometric terms of type
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$\gamma ^m \delta ^n$$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:mrow>
                            <mml:msup>
                              <mml:mi>γ</mml:mi>
                              <mml:mi>m</mml:mi>
                            </mml:msup>
                            <mml:msup>
                              <mml:mi>δ</mml:mi>
                              <mml:mi>n</mml:mi>
                            </mml:msup>
                          </mml:mrow>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    . Using a transform-based approach, we prove that this is certainly the case
                    <jats:italic>if</jats:italic>
                    the steady-state joint probability generating function
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$U(z_1,z_2)$$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:mrow>
                            <mml:mi>U</mml:mi>
                            <mml:mo>(</mml:mo>
                            <mml:msub>
                              <mml:mi>z</mml:mi>
                              <mml:mn>1</mml:mn>
                            </mml:msub>
                            <mml:mo>,</mml:mo>
                            <mml:msub>
                              <mml:mi>z</mml:mi>
                              <mml:mn>2</mml:mn>
                            </mml:msub>
                            <mml:mo>)</mml:mo>
                          </mml:mrow>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    of the two system contents can be expressed as a bivariate
                    <jats:italic>rational</jats:italic>
                    function of its two arguments, with mutually prime numerator and denominator, whereby the denominator is the
                    <jats:italic>product</jats:italic>
                    of two univariate polynomials in
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$z_1$$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:msub>
                            <mml:mi>z</mml:mi>
                            <mml:mn>1</mml:mn>
                          </mml:msub>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    and
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$z_2$$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:msub>
                            <mml:mi>z</mml:mi>
                            <mml:mn>2</mml:mn>
                          </mml:msub>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    , respectively, whose zeroes
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$\hat{z_1}$$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:mover>
                            <mml:msub>
                              <mml:mi>z</mml:mi>
                              <mml:mn>1</mml:mn>
                            </mml:msub>
                            <mml:mo>^</mml:mo>
                          </mml:mover>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    and
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$\hat{z_2}$$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:mover>
                            <mml:msub>
                              <mml:mi>z</mml:mi>
                              <mml:mn>2</mml:mn>
                            </mml:msub>
                            <mml:mo>^</mml:mo>
                          </mml:mover>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    all have
                    <jats:italic>multiplicity one</jats:italic>
                    . We show that the decay rates
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$\gamma $$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:mi>γ</mml:mi>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    and
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$\delta $$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:mi>δ</mml:mi>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    appearing in
                    <jats:italic>u</jats:italic>
                    (
                    <jats:italic>m</jats:italic>
                    , 
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                    ) are the inverse values of (some of) the zeroes
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$\hat{z_1}$$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:mover>
                            <mml:msub>
                              <mml:mi>z</mml:mi>
                              <mml:mn>1</mml:mn>
                            </mml:msub>
                            <mml:mo>^</mml:mo>
                          </mml:mover>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    and
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$\hat{z_2}$$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:mover>
                            <mml:msub>
                              <mml:mi>z</mml:mi>
                              <mml:mn>2</mml:mn>
                            </mml:msub>
                            <mml:mo>^</mml:mo>
                          </mml:mover>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    , but, in general, there may be zero-pairs
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$(\hat{z_1}, \hat{z_2})$$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:mrow>
                            <mml:mo>(</mml:mo>
                            <mml:mover>
                              <mml:msub>
                                <mml:mi>z</mml:mi>
                                <mml:mn>1</mml:mn>
                              </mml:msub>
                              <mml:mo>^</mml:mo>
                            </mml:mover>
                            <mml:mo>,</mml:mo>
                            <mml:mover>
                              <mml:msub>
                                <mml:mi>z</mml:mi>
                                <mml:mn>2</mml:mn>
                              </mml:msub>
                              <mml:mo>^</mml:mo>
                            </mml:mover>
                            <mml:mo>)</mml:mo>
                          </mml:mrow>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    that do not contribute a bivariate geometric term in
                    <jats:italic>u</jats:italic>
                    (
                    <jats:italic>m</jats:italic>
                    , 
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                    ). For two specific
                    <jats:italic>classes</jats:italic>
                    of
                    <jats:italic>discrete-time</jats:italic>
                    two-queue systems, we prove that, when
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$U(z_1,z_2)$$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:mrow>
                            <mml:mi>U</mml:mi>
                            <mml:mo>(</mml:mo>
                            <mml:msub>
                              <mml:mi>z</mml:mi>
                              <mml:mn>1</mml:mn>
                            </mml:msub>
                            <mml:mo>,</mml:mo>
                            <mml:msub>
                              <mml:mi>z</mml:mi>
                              <mml:mn>2</mml:mn>
                            </mml:msub>
                            <mml:mo>)</mml:mo>
                          </mml:mrow>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    has the prescribed form, only the zero-pairs that are
                    <jats:italic>zero-tuples of the kernel</jats:italic>
                    of the system contribute a term in
                    <jats:italic>u</jats:italic>
                    (
                    <jats:italic>m</jats:italic>
                    , 
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                    ). In an extended series of examples, we then demonstrate that, within the two classes, specific instances (corresponding with specific arrival processes) that comply with the condition on
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$U(z_1,z_2)$$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:mrow>
                            <mml:mi>U</mml:mi>
                            <mml:mo>(</mml:mo>
                            <mml:msub>
                              <mml:mi>z</mml:mi>
                              <mml:mn>1</mml:mn>
                            </mml:msub>
                            <mml:mo>,</mml:mo>
                            <mml:msub>
                              <mml:mi>z</mml:mi>
                              <mml:mn>2</mml:mn>
                            </mml:msub>
                            <mml:mo>)</mml:mo>
                          </mml:mrow>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    indeed exist. In some examples, we can use existing solutions, but in other cases, we also construct entirely new solutions, thereby identifying several new
                    <jats:italic>solvable</jats:italic>
                    two-queue models. We observe that, in most cases, the zero-pairs that do contribute terms in
                    <jats:italic>u</jats:italic>
                    (
                    <jats:italic>m</jats:italic>
                    , 
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                    ) are mutually
                    <jats:italic>connected</jats:italic>
                    , in the sense that each of them has its first or second component in common with at least one other pair that contributes, but we also construct a remarkable example where this is not the case.
                  </jats:p>
title: Coupled queues whose interior stationary joint content distribution is a finite sum of bivariate geometric terms

items.abstract: <jats:p>We construct a stationary ergodic process $X_{1},X_{2},\ldots$ such that each $X_{t}$ has the uniform distribution on the unit square and the length $L_{n}$ of the shortest path through the points $X_{1},X_{2},\ldots,X_{n}$ is not asymptotic to a constant times the square root of $n$. In other words, we show that the Beardwood, Halton, and Hammersley [Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. 55 (1959) 299–327] theorem does not extend from the case of independent uniformly distributed random variables to the case of stationary ergodic sequences with uniform marginal distributions.</jats:p>
title: Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley theorem for stationary ergodic sequences: A counterexample
